newsitem.title: USA: Fla. atty gen predicts tobacco deal as talks resume.
newsitem.headline: Fla. atty gen predicts tobacco deal as talks resume.

text.p: Tobacco litigation talks are resuming in New York this week and one prominent state attorney general predicted Tuesday that a draft settlement proposal could be reached within two to three weeks.

The prediction by Florida Attorney General Robert Buttterworth comes as negotiators are under intense pressure ahead of the first trial to decide whether manufacturers must reimburse states for Medicaid health care costs of smokers.

Butterworth told reporters in Tallahassee that significant progress is being made and that he expected a draft proposal could be reached within two to three weeks. He said both sides had reached tentative agreements covering sharp advertising restrictions and Food and Drug Administration oversight of the tobacco industry.
"I think a structure could be in place that we could bring back to the attorneys general in the country," he said.

Butterworth said negotiators had reached agreement, subject to a complete pact, that cigarette companies would end all outdoor advertising such as billboards and put in place a campaign aimed at reducing cigarette use by teenagers.
He said any pact would require congressional approval, which could possibly be obtained by year's end.

On Friday, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, the lead negotiator for the states, cautioned that a final deal was not imminent. He told Reuters he thought he would know within two weeks whether a deal could be reached and said that if inadequate progress were made, he would leave the talks to prepare for trial.
Mississippi's case against the industry is scheduled to be the first to go to trial on July 7, with Florida to follow on August 4.

If the talks were to be suspended, it would leave the industry facing hundreds of lawsuits throughout the country with the number of filings steadily rising. Although the industry has won most of the cases filed in the past, the risks are much higher due to different legal theories and the availability of internal documents about the industry's knowledge of nicotine and other potential health problems.

Legal experts say the biggest threat to the industry at present are the Medicaid suits filed by 29 state attorneys general seeking to recoup health care costs of smokers. Similar suits have been filed by a number of municipalities, including New York City, San Francisco and Los Angeles County.

A group of attorneys general, plaintiffs lawyers and representatives of the health community began negotiating with the tobacco industry in early April in an effort to resolve mounting litigation against manufacturers in exchange for major health and monetary concessions.

In addition to the Medicaid cases, the industry is facing its first class action trial, beginning June 2 in Miami. The suit is seeking damages on behalf of about 60,000 flight attendants who allegedly contracted lung diseases and other ailments from secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger jets.

While Moore said the talks have focused so far on health care issues, including government regulation of the tobacco industry and smoking reduction programmes, the key hurdle is whether an acceptable plan can be created that would give the industry certainty about how much it would have to pay for injuries while preserving individuals' right to sue.

The negotiations have drawn wide-spread criticism from some members of Congress and health groups who worry that a sweetheart deal will be reached that will provide inadequate health safeguards and will not punish the industry for alleged wrongdoing. The American Medical Society is hosting a meeting of health groups on Wednesday to address such concerns.
"How can anyone barter the public health for peanuts by permitting this industry to coninue manufacturing an addictive lethal drug?" said Gordon Draves of Georgians Against Smoking Pollution.
However, Moore said the effort to end underage smoking is a top priority.
"I contemplate when we're finished this industry will be regulated tighter than they have ever contemplated and tighter than the FDA ever contemplated," he said.
"Our top priority is to reduce teenage consumption by 50 percent in seven years. If we do that, then that will reduce adult consumption within 15 to 20 years by the same amount," he said.
